ety.text: From Middle English to (“also, in addition to”), from Old English tō (“furthermore, also, besides”), adverbial use of preposition tō (“to, into”). The sense of "in addition, also" deriving from the original meaning of "apart, separately" (compare Old English prefix tō- (“apart”)). Doublet of to; see there for more.

senses.d: Likewise.
Also, in addition marks a statement as equally valid as the preceding one.
ex: There has been a cutback in federal subsidies. Rates have been increasing too.
He's always willing to help. He, too, is generous with his time.

senses.d: To an excessive degree, more than enough indicates that the degree of a quality is more than what is needed or wanted.
ex: Near-synonyms: extremely, unnecessarily, all too
I'm still much too young to drive, and my grandpa is already far too old.

senses.d: To a high degree, very.
ex: She doesn't talk too much.  I'm not too sure about this.

senses.d: Used to contradict a negative assertion with present and simple past forms of be, do, and auxiliary verbs
ex: You're not old enough yet. ― I am too!
You can't jump that fence. ― Can too jump it!

senses.d: Used for emphasis, without reference to any previous statement.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French aussi, from Old French ossi, ausi, alsi (“as, in the same way as”), from Vulgar Latin *ale si (“other so, else so”), from Latin alid, aliud (“other, another, any other, else”) + sīc (“so, thus”); probably a calque of Frankish *allswā (“as, likewise, in the same way”).

Assuming that anco represents the original form, likely a rebracketing of ancora as anc'ora. A borrowing from Old Occitan ancui (“on this day”) has also been suggested, but this would explain neither the stress position of anche, nor the lack of a final -ui (an acceptable ending in Italian; cf. lui).
Inherited from Latin pūrē, the adverb of pūrus.

ety.text: From Middle English tool, tol, from Old English tōl (“tool, implement, instrument”, literally “that with which one prepares something”), perhaps borrowed from Old Norse tól, but at any rate ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tōlą (“that which is used in preparation, tool”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewh₂- (“to tie to, secure”), equivalent to taw (“to prepare”) + -le (agent suffix). Cognate with Scots tuil (“tool, implement, instrument, device”), Icelandic tól (“tool”), Faroese tól (“tool, instrument”).

ex: Several prehistoric tools, including a stone ax, were found during the dig.
